arguments.name: Consumer Messaging Test for Marine vs Disaster Preparedness
arguments.method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Recruit 400 respondents: 200 marine recreational users (boaters, campers) and 200 homeowners in disaster-prone regions. Randomly assign participants to one of two message conditions: Marine Condition (safety for extended trips, remote areas) or Disaster Condition (emergency preparedness, disasters). Both conditions present a consumer-grade 406 MHz PLB at a fixed price of $150. Measure purchase intent (binary: would buy) and willingness to pay (WTP) on a 7-point scale.
arguments.sample: 400 respondents (200 marine recreational users, 200 homeowners in disaster-prone regions).
arguments.measure: Purchase intent (binary) and willingness to pay (WTP) on a 7-point scale.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Marine condition will generate higher purchase intent and WTP than disaster condition.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Disaster condition will generate higher purchase intent and WTP than marine condition.

arguments.decision_rule: If purchase intent in the Marine Condition group is at least 15 percentage points higher than in the Disaster Condition group, proceed with a marine-focused consumer proposition. If purchase intent in the Disaster Condition group is at least 15 percentage points higher, proceed with a disaster‑focused proposition. If the difference is ≤ 15 percentage points, no expansion is recommended.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

arguments.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. Public sources show the 406 MHz PLB is intended for general public use in life-threatening situations, not for marine recreational users. Evidence of consumer demand is lacking; a proposed test (X1) is needed to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay for marine recreational users.

Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. Public sources show the 406 MHz PLB is intended for general public use in life-threatening situations, not for marine recreational users. Evidence of consumer demand is lacking; a proposed test (X1) is needed to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay for marine recreational users.
arguments.target_customer: Marine recreational users (boaters, campers, hikers) who need reliable emergency communication in remote areas.
arguments.value_proposition: A consumer-grade 406 MHz satellite distress beacon that guarantees rescue in life-threatening situations, marketed as a safety necessity for extended trips and remote areas.
arguments.next_action: Run the proposed Consumer Messaging Test (X1) to compare purchase intent and willingness to pay for marine recreational users versus homeowners in disaster-prone regions.
arguments.uncertainty: The size of the marine recreational market and willingness to pay a premium for a consumer-grade PLB are uncertain. Regulatory feasibility and competitive landscape are also unknown.
would_change_if: If the test shows purchase intent for marine recreational users is at least 15 percentage points higher than for homeowners in disaster-prone regions, we would recommend a marine-focused consumer proposition.
If the test shows no significant difference or lower intent, we would recommend no expansion and continue focusing on B2B customers.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence from public sources available by late 2002 to justify ACR Electronics investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case built on its 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before late 2002; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must identify evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, and competitive landscape for a consumer product.
Must consider ACR’s existing B2B products (shipping, aircraft, military, marine) and its current reach to individual buyers.
Must assess regulatory and market feasibility of a consumer product using satellite distress beacons.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting individual users (e.g., marine recreational users, outdoor enthusiasts) with a dedicated product line and marketing.
2) Expand the existing B2B product line into adjacent consumer segments without a differentiated proposition (e.g., add a consumer‑focused version of the beacon for marine recreational users).
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on current B2B customers and existing product portfolio.
4) License the 406 MHz technology to third‑party manufacturers for consumer products, capturing value through royalties rather than direct consumer sales.

T1.why_behaviour_changes: These users currently lack affordable, reliable ways to signal distress when lost or in danger, and they would switch to a consumer beacon if it is affordable, easy to use, and backed by a rescue track record.
T1.how_value_is_captured: ACR would sell a differentiated consumer product line through marine retailers and online channels, capturing value through premium pricing justified by the rescue capability and brand trust.
assumptions: Marine recreational users are willing to pay a premium for a reliable distress beacon.
The 406 MHz technology meets or exceeds the FCC's safety and performance standards for consumer use.
ACR can reach these users through existing marine retail channels or new online distribution.

Sales of a consumer beacon will be concentrated in regions with high boating activity (e.g., Florida, Alaska).
Competitive products will be priced lower than ACR's proposed consumer line, limiting market share.

X1.name: Willingness-to-Pay Survey for Marine vs. Outdoor Recreational Users
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios to measure willingness to pay for a consumer personal locator beacon. Participants are recruited from two target segments: marine recreational users (boaters, campers) and outdoor recreational users (hikers, campers, disaster preparedness enthusiasts). Each participant sees a product description and price, and is asked to indicate their maximum price they would pay.
X1.sample: Proposed sample: 200 participants (100 marine recreational users, 100 outdoor recreational users), recruited via online panels. Stratified by region (Florida, Alaska, national parks) to reflect high activity areas.
X1.measure: Maximum price participants would pay for the beacon, and intent to purchase (binary: "Would buy at this price?" or "Would not buy at this price?").

prediction_by_theory.T1: Marine recreational users will report willingness to pay at least $50 and higher intent to purchase than outdoor recreational users.

arguments.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence from public sources available by late 2002 to justify ACR Electronics investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case built on its 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology.

position.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. Public sources show the 406 MHz PLB is intended for general public use in life-threatening situations, but they do not demonstrate consumer demand, willingness to pay, or competitive landscape. Run the proposed Consumer Preference Test to validate whether safety messaging drives purchase intent and willingness to pay before committing resources.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence from public sources available by late 2002 to justify ACR Electronics investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case built on its 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before late 2002; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must identify evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, and competitive landscape for a consumer product.
Must consider ACR’s existing B2B products (shipping, aircraft, military, marine) and its current reach to individual buyers.
Must assess regulatory and market feasibility of a consumer product using satellite distress beacons.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting individual users (e.g., marine recreational users, outdoor enthusiasts) with a dedicated product line and marketing.
2) Expand the existing B2B product line into adjacent consumer segments without a differentiated proposition (e.g., add a consumer‑focused version of the beacon for marine recreational users).
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on current B2B customers and existing product portfolio.
4) License the 406 MHz technology to third‑party manufacturers for consumer products, capturing value through royalties rather than direct consumer sales.

T1.claim: Individual users will purchase a consumer-grade 406 MHz satellite distress beacon because they perceive it as a life-saving safety device for remote emergency situations, and they are willing to pay a premium for peace of mind.
T1.who_benefits: Individual outdoor enthusiasts, marine recreational users, and emergency-prepared campers who face high-risk environments without reliable communication.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: The beacon provides a reliable way to signal for help in areas where traditional communication fails, reducing fear of being stranded and increasing trust in the technology.
T1.how_value_is_captured: ACR can sell a differentiated consumer product at a premium price through retail channels, capturing margin on hardware and branding.
assumptions: There is a measurable segment of individuals who frequently engage in high-risk outdoor activities and are willing to invest in emergency preparedness.
Regulatory requirements (FCC/NOAA) allow consumer use of 406 MHz PLBs without significant additional certification costs.
Marketing can effectively communicate the safety benefit to this segment.
predictions: In a survey of target consumers, at least 30% would indicate intent to purchase a consumer-grade PLB within 12 months at a price above $100.
Sales of a consumer product would be concentrated in regions with high outdoor recreation activity (e.g., Alaska, Hawaii, coastal states).
T1.first_claim: Individual users will purchase a consumer-grade 406 MHz satellite distress beacon because they perceive it as a life-saving safety device for remote emergency situations, and they are willing to pay a premium for peace of mind.

T2.claim: Individual users will purchase a consumer-grade 406 MHz satellite distress beacon because it is a convenient, one‑time purchase that eliminates the need to carry separate emergency devices, and they value the convenience of a single device for multiple uses.
T2.who_benefits: Individual outdoor enthusiasts and marine recreational users who already carry multiple safety devices and prefer a single, integrated solution.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: The beacon reduces the cognitive load of managing multiple devices and the cost of replacing batteries or accessories, making it attractive for a one‑time purchase.
T2.how_value_is_captured: ACR can sell a bundled consumer product at a lower unit price than selling individual components, capturing volume sales through retail channels.
assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay a premium for convenience over multiple devices.
The beacon can be marketed as a single, easy‑to‑use product rather than a collection of separate items.
Distribution channels (retail, online) can reach the target segment effectively.
predictions: In a survey, at least 25% of target consumers would indicate intent to purchase a bundled consumer product within 12 months at a price below $150.
Sales would be concentrated in regions with high outdoor recreation activity where multiple devices are already carried.
T2.first_claim: Individual users will purchase a consumer-grade 406 MHz satellite distress beacon because it is a convenient, one‑time purchase that eliminates the need to carry separate emergency devices, and they value the convenience of a single device for multiple uses.

X1.name: Consumer Preference Test: Safety vs Convenience Messaging
X1.method: Online survey with simulated product offers and willingness-to-pay (WTP) questions.
X1.sample: 300 respondents recruited from outdoor recreation and marine enthusiast forums in the U.S. and Canada, balanced for age and gender.
X1.measure: Percentage of respondents who indicate intent to purchase at each price point (under $150 for convenience, above $150 for safety) and average WTP per price point.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Safety messaging will generate higher purchase intent and WTP at prices above $150, and purchase intent will be concentrated in high-risk regions.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Convenience messaging will generate higher purchase intent and WTP at prices under $150, and purchase intent will be concentrated in regions with multiple device ownership.

X1.decision_rule: If the proportion of respondents indicating intent to purchase at the safety price point exceeds 35% and the average WTP at that price point exceeds $120, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition emphasizing safety. If the convenience price point exceeds 35% and the average WTP at that price point exceeds $80, develop a convenience-focused proposition. If neither condition is met, do not expand.

revisions.reason: Simulated evidence about a label printer reducing packing errors does not address consumer purchase motivations, willingness to pay, or the safety versus convenience proposition. Therefore it does not affect T1.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. Public sources show the 406 MHz PLB is intended for general public use in life-threatening situations, but they do not demonstrate consumer demand, willingness to pay, or competitive landscape. Run the proposed Consumer Preference Test to validate whether safety messaging drives purchase intent and willingness to pay before committing resources.
final.target_customer: Individual outdoor enthusiasts, marine recreational users, and emergency-prepared campers who face high-risk environments without reliable communication.
final.value_proposition: A differentiated consumer product that provides a reliable way to signal for help in remote emergency situations, marketed as a life-saving safety device.
final.next_action: Execute the Consumer Preference Test (300 respondents, $18,000, 8 weeks) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay under safety versus convenience messaging.
final.uncertainty: The size of the consumer market, actual willingness to pay, and the competitive landscape for a consumer-grade PLB are uncertain. The test will resolve these uncertainties.
would_change_if: If the test shows purchase intent at the safety price point exceeds 35% and average WTP exceeds $120, we would proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition emphasizing safety.
If the test shows purchase intent at the convenience price point exceeds 35% and average WTP exceeds $80, we would develop a convenience-focused proposition.
If neither condition is met, we would maintain the current focus on B2B customers and existing product portfolio.

position.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that positions the 406 MHz beacon as a life-saving safety device for marine recreational users and outdoor enthusiasts, emphasizing NOAA/RTCM compliance and rescue capability. Use the proposed Consumer Propension Test to validate willingness to pay and purchase intent before full-scale launch.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence from public sources available by late 2002 to justify ACR Electronics investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case built on its 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before late 2002; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must identify evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, and competitive landscape for a consumer product.
Must consider ACR’s existing B2B products (shipping, aircraft, military, marine) and its current reach to individual buyers.
Must assess regulatory and market feasibility of a consumer product using satellite distress beacons.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting individual users (e.g., marine recreational users, outdoor enthusiasts) with a dedicated product line and marketing.
2) Expand the existing B2B product line into adjacent consumer segments without a differentiated proposition (e.g., add a consumer‑focused version of the beacon for marine recreational users).
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on current B2B customers and existing product portfolio.
4) License the 406 MHz technology to third‑party manufacturers for consumer products, capturing value through royalties rather than direct consumer sales.

T1.claim: Individual users will adopt a consumer personal locator beacon primarily for safety and rescue, not for fashion or multiple ownership, so a differentiated consumer proposition will generate demand only if the device is positioned as a life-saving tool for marine recreational users and outdoor enthusiasts.
T1.who_benefits: Marine recreational users, outdoor enthusiasts, and their families who need reliable distress signaling in remote environments.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: These users face high-risk activities where a single distress signal can mean the difference between rescue and survival; they will purchase a beacon if it reliably sends a signal and is affordable enough to buy once.
T1.how_value_is_captured: ACR captures value through direct consumer sales of a differentiated product line, pricing it at a premium justified by safety and rescue capability, and potentially through accessories or service contracts.
assumptions: The 406 MHz beacon is perceived as reliable and effective for distress signaling in remote marine and outdoor settings.
Regulatory requirements (NOAA registration, RTCM standards) do not prevent consumer sales.
Willingness to pay for a safety device is sufficient to offset the cost of a differentiated consumer product.
predictions: In a test offering a consumer-oriented beacon to marine recreational users, purchase intent or actual purchases will be higher than for a generic EPIRB sold through retail channels.
Surveyed users will cite safety and rescue as the primary reason for purchase, not fashion or multiple ownership.

X1.name: Consumer Propension Test: Safety vs Convenience Messaging
X1.method: Recruit 200 adult participants (100 marine recreationalists and 100 outdoor enthusiasts) via an online panel. Randomly assign participants to one of two message conditions: Safety Condition (emphasizing life-saving rescue capability and NOAA/RTCM compliance) or Convenience Condition (emphasizing easy-to-use, portable design and immediate distress signaling). After exposure, ask participants to indicate purchase intent (yes/no) and maximum price they would pay (willingness to pay).
X1.sample: 200 adult participants (100 marine recreationalists and 100 outdoor enthusiasts) recruited from an online panel.
X1.measure: Purchase intent (yes/no) and willingness to pay (maximum price) in each condition.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Safety Condition will generate higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than Convenience Condition.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Convenience Condition will generate higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than Safety Condition.

X1.decision_rule: If the average willingness to pay in the Safety Condition is at least 20% higher than in the Convenience Condition, we conclude T1 is more likely. If the difference is less than 20% or the Safety Condition shows no higher willingness to pay, we conclude T2 is more likely. If both conditions show similar willingness to pay, we conclude neither theory is supported and recommend further market research.

arguments.name: Consumer Propension Test: Safety vs Convenience Messaging
arguments.method: Recruit 200 adult participants (100 marine recreationalists and 100 outdoor enthusiasts) via an online panel. Randomly assign participants to one of two message conditions: Safety Condition (emphasizing life-saving rescue capability and NOAA/RTCM compliance) or Convenience Condition (emphasizing easy-to-use, portable design and immediate distress signaling). After exposure, ask participants to indicate purchase intent (yes/no) and maximum price they would pay (willingness to pay).
arguments.sample: 200 adult participants (100 marine recreationalists and 100 outdoor enthusiasts) recruited from an online panel.
arguments.measure: Purchase intent (yes/no) and willingness to pay (maximum price) in each condition.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Safety Condition will generate higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than Convenience Condition.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Convenience Condition will generate higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than Safety Condition.

arguments.decision_rule: If the average willingness to pay in the Safety Condition is at least 20% higher than in the Convenience Condition, we conclude T1 is more likely. If the difference is less than 20% or the Safety Condition shows no higher willingness to pay, we conclude T2 is more likely. If both conditions show similar willingness to pay, we conclude neither theory is supported and recommend further market research.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

frame.objective: Determine whether Deere & Company should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, leveraging its tractor engineering, based on evidence available in mid-1962.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before mid-1962; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must identify evidence that justifies the investment, such as market demand, technical feasibility, or competitive advantage.
Consider the existing B2B2C model of independent dealer distribution and the current reach to individual buyers.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., small‑scale landscaping, hobby farming, or homeowner tasks) using tractor engineering.
2) Expand the existing B2B2C model by deepening dealer relationships and offering additional service or parts to individual buyers without a new differentiated proposition.
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on the current B2B2C model of farm and industrial equipment sold through independent dealers.
4) Target a different customer group (e.g., small‑farm owners, urban gardeners, or DIY enthusiasts) with a proposition tailored to their needs, using the same tractor platform.

The market for small‑scale landscaping is growing sufficiently to support a differentiated proposition.
Deere can differentiate its product through design, performance, and brand positioning.
predictions: A test offering a differentiated lawn tractor to homeowners will generate higher purchase intent and higher conversion rates compared to a standard garden attachment.

X1.method: Online survey with randomized exposure to a differentiated lawn tractor proposition. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups: Group A sees a standard garden attachment description and is asked about purchase intent and willingness to pay a premium; Group B sees a differentiated lawn tractor description emphasizing single, integrated functionality and premium pricing. Both groups are asked the same final question: "Would you purchase this differentiated lawn tractor at a premium price?"
X1.sample: 300 homeowners with small gardens, recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, income, and prior garden equipment ownership.
X1.measure: Purchase intent (binary: would purchase) and willingness to pay a premium (willingness-to-pay scale).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Group A will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay a premium than Group B.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Group B will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay a premium than Group A.

X1.decision_rule: If Group B's purchase intent exceeds Group A's by at least 10 percentage points, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition. If Group A's purchase intent exceeds Group B's by at least 10 percentage points, maintain the current B2B2C model. If the difference is within 10 points, conduct a smaller follow-up survey to validate the results before committing resources.

final.value_proposition: A differentiated lawn tractor that combines Deere’s engineering expertise with a single, integrated solution, offering superior performance, durability, and brand reliability at a premium price.
final.next_action: Run the proposed Consumer Proposition Test (300 homeowners, 8 weeks, €15,000) to compare purchase intent and willingness to pay a premium between a standard garden attachment description and a differentiated lawn tractor description.
final.uncertainty: The size of the consumer market for small-scale landscaping and the willingness of homeowners to pay a premium for a differentiated proposition are uncertain. The test will resolve these uncertainties.
would_change_if: If the test shows purchase intent for the differentiated proposition is significantly lower than for a standard garden attachment, we would reconsider the investment and focus on the existing B2B2C model.

If new evidence shows strong consumer demand for premium-priced lawn tractors, we would reconsider the premium positioning.

frame.objective: Determine whether Deere & Company should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, leveraging its tractor engineering, based on evidence available in mid-1962.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before mid-1962; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must identify evidence that justifies the investment, such as market demand, technical feasibility, or competitive advantage.
Consider the existing B2B2C model of independent dealer distribution and the current reach to individual buyers.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., small‑scale landscaping, hobby farming, or homeowner tasks) using tractor engineering.
2) Expand the existing B2B2C model by deepening dealer relationships and offering additional service or parts to individual buyers without a new differentiated proposition.
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on the current B2B2C model of farm and industrial equipment sold through independent dealers.
4) Target a different customer group (e.g., small‑farm owners, urban gardeners, or DIY enthusiasts) with a proposition tailored to their needs, using the same tractor platform.

Deere can differentiate its lawn tractor from competitors through design and performance.

position.recommendation: Invest in a limited pilot test of a differentiated lawn tractor proposition targeting homeowners with small gardens, using independent dealers to promote and service the product. The pilot should measure purchase intent and conversion rates to determine whether homeowners are willing to adopt a differentiated proposition.

frame.objective: Determine whether Deere & Company should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, leveraging its tractor engineering, based on evidence available in mid-1962.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before mid-1962; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must identify evidence that justifies the investment, such as market demand, technical feasibility, or competitive advantage.
Consider the existing B2B2C model of independent dealer distribution and the current reach to individual buyers.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., small‑scale landscaping, hobby farming, or homeowner tasks) using tractor engineering.
2) Expand the existing B2B2C model by deepening dealer relationships and offering additional service or parts to individual buyers without a new differentiated proposition.
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on the current B2B2C model of farm and industrial equipment sold through independent dealers.
4) Target a different customer group (e.g., small‑farm owners, urban gardeners, or DIY enthusiasts) with a proposition tailored to their needs, using the same tractor platform.

T1.claim: Homeowners will adopt a differentiated lawn tractor proposition because they view it as a convenient, single‑tool solution for small‑scale landscaping and gardening, and they trust the brand for durability and reliability.
T1.who_benefits: Individual homeowners with small gardens who need a single tool for mowing, weeding, and light cleanup.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: They shift from multiple tools or manual labor to a single, easy‑to‑use machine that can handle multiple tasks, reducing time and effort.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Deere captures value by selling a differentiated model at a premium price through independent dealers, leveraging its tractor engineering to offer superior performance and durability.
assumptions: Homeowners are willing to pay a premium for a single, integrated tool.
Independent dealers can effectively promote and service a differentiated consumer proposition.
The market size for small‑scale landscaping is sufficient to justify production and marketing investment.
predictions: A test offering a differentiated lawn tractor to homeowners will generate higher purchase intent and higher conversion rates compared to a generic garden tool.
Sales of the differentiated model will be concentrated among homeowners with small gardens, not large‑scale commercial users.

X1.name: Differentiated Lawn Tractor Test
X1.method: Run a limited pilot in two independent dealer locations (one served primarily by small‑farm owners, one by homeowners) offering a differentiated lawn tractor model at a premium price. Track purchase intent (surveyed), conversion rate (number of signed orders), and customer demographics. Use a control group of a generic garden tool to compare.
X1.sample: 20 homes (10 small‑farm owners, 10 homeowners) and 20 small‑farm owners, randomly assigned to either the differentiated lawn tractor or the generic garden tool. Each location has 10 dealer contacts to reach potential buyers.
X1.measure: Purchase intent (1‑5 scale) and conversion rate (percentage of contacts who place an order). Also collect demographic data (age, garden size, prior ownership of a lawn tractor).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Homeowners will show higher purchase intent and conversion rates than small‑farm owners, because they seek a single, convenient tool for small‑scale landscaping.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Small‑farm owners will show higher purchase intent and conversion rates than homeowners, because they need a versatile tool for multiple tasks.

X1.decision_rule: If the differentiated lawn tractor converts at least 10% of its target contacts (e.g., 2 homeowner orders and 2 small‑farm owner orders) and homeowner conversion exceeds small‑farm owner conversion by at least 15 percentage points, proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition. If not, maintain the existing B2B2C model.

revisions.reason: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns a label printer reducing packing errors and does not address homeowner adoption of a differentiated lawn tractor proposition. Therefore it does not affect T1.

final.recommendation: Invest in a limited pilot test of a differentiated lawn tractor proposition targeting homeowners with small gardens, using independent dealers to promote and service the product. The pilot should measure purchase intent and conversion rates to determine whether homeowners are willing to adopt a differentiated proposition.
final.target_customer: Homeowners with small gardens who need a single, convenient tool for mowing, weeding, and light cleanup.
final.value_proposition: A differentiated lawn tractor that leverages Deere’s tractor engineering to offer superior performance, durability, and ease of use, sold through independent dealers at a premium price.
final.next_action: Run the proposed 12‑week pilot with 20 homes (10 small‑farm owners, 10 homeowners) and 20 small‑farm owners, randomly assigned to either the differentiated lawn tractor or a generic garden tool. Track purchase intent and conversion rates.
final.uncertainty: The willingness of homeowners to pay a premium for a differentiated proposition is uncertain. The pilot will determine whether homeowners will adopt the proposition and whether they are willing to pay a premium.
would_change_if: If the pilot shows that small‑farm owners show higher purchase intent and conversion rates than homeowners, or if homeowner conversion falls below a threshold (e.g., <10%), we would reconsider the investment and explore alternative customer

If new evidence shows that the lawn tractor market was already saturated by 1962 and small‑farm owners were the primary buyers, we would abandon the differentiated consumer proposition and focus on the existing B2B2C model.

position.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for small-scale landscaping, leveraging Deere’s tractor engineering. The evidence shows growing demand for garden tractors as inexpensive, practical tools for small gardens, and the company already produced a consumer model in 1963. A test should measure willingness to pay and purchase intent for a convenience‑focused model versus a status‑focused one.

frame.objective: Determine whether Deere & Company should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, leveraging its tractor engineering, based on evidence available in mid-1962.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before mid-1962; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must identify evidence that justifies the investment, such as market demand, technical feasibility, or competitive advantage.
Consider the existing B2B2C model of independent dealer distribution and the current reach to individual buyers.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., small‑scale landscaping, hobby farming, or homeowner tasks) using tractor engineering.
2) Expand the existing B2B2C model by deepening dealer relationships and offering additional service or parts to individual buyers without a new differentiated proposition.
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on the current B2B2C model of farm and industrial equipment sold through independent dealers.
4) Target a different customer group (e.g., small‑farm owners, urban gardeners, or DIY enthusiasts) with a proposition tailored to their needs, using the same tractor platform.

T1.claim: Homeowners will adopt garden tractors because they view them as a convenient, single‑tool solution for small‑scale landscaping and yard work, reducing the need for multiple tools and labor.
T1.who_benefits: Individual homeowners who need to clear grass, rake leaves, or move mulch without hiring help.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: The growing household garden size and the perception of tractors as inexpensive and easy to maintain make them an attractive, one‑time purchase rather than a series of tools.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Deere can capture value by selling a differentiated consumer model at a premium price, leveraging its tractor engineering to offer durability and performance that justify higher cost.
assumptions: Homeowners in 1962 have sufficient disposable income to purchase a garden tractor.
The market for small‑scale landscaping is large enough to support a consumer line.
Deere can produce a consumer‑grade tractor that meets homeowner expectations for ease of use and durability.
predictions: A survey of homeowners would show higher intent to buy a garden tractor than a comparable farm tractor.
Sales of a consumer‑focused model would be higher in regions with larger household gardens.
Customers would cite convenience and cost savings as primary purchase reasons.
T1.first_claim: Homeowners will adopt garden tractors because they view them as a convenient, single‑tool solution for small‑scale landscaping and yard work, reducing the need for multiple tools and labor.

T2.claim: Homeowners will adopt garden tractors because they view them as a status symbol and status signal, indicating modernity and capability, especially among middle‑class households.
T2.who_benefits: Middle‑class homeowners who want to demonstrate financial stability and modern living standards.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: The 1960s consumer culture emphasizes ownership of modern, convenient goods; a garden tractor becomes a visible marker of success and ability to manage a garden.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Deere can capture value by positioning a consumer model as a premium, status‑friendly product, justifying higher price through brand prestige and design.
assumptions: Middle‑class households in 1962 value visible status and modernity.
A garden tractor can be marketed as a status item rather than a utilitarian tool.
Deere can design and price a model that appeals to status‑conscious buyers.
predictions: A survey of homeowners would rank garden tractors higher for status than for practical utility.
Sales would be concentrated in regions where middle‑class households are more visible.
Customers would cite status and prestige as primary purchase reasons.
T2.first_claim: Homeowners will adopt garden tractors because they view them as a status symbol and status signal, indicating modernity and capability, especially among middle‑class households.

assessments.quote: the demand for garden tractors was rapidly increasing as households with small gardens found them rather inexpensive, practical to use for a variety of chores, and they were economical to maintain.
assessments.does_not_show: It does not show that homeowners will purchase a garden tractor, nor that Deere would capture value from a consumer proposition.

assessments.does_not_show: It does not address whether homeowners purchase garden tractors for status or status signal; it only notes the existence of a prototype.

X1.name: Consumer Proposition Preference Test
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios and stated reasons.
X1.sample: 500 U.S. homeowners aged 30-55, recruited via panels, balanced across regions with varying garden sizes.
X1.measure: 1) Willingness to pay (WTP) for a consumer‑focused garden tractor. 2) Primary purchase reason (convenience vs. status). 3) Intent to purchase (binary: would buy).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher WTP and purchase intent among homeowners with small gardens and those citing convenience as primary reason.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher WTP and purchase intent among middle‑class homeowners and those citing status as primary reason.

X1.decision_rule: If the average WTP for the convenience‑focused model exceeds the WTP for the status‑focused model by at least 15% and the purchase intent difference is at least 10 percentage points, proceed with the differentiated consumer proposition. Otherwise, do not invest.

revisions.reason: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns a label printer reducing packing errors and does not address homeowner motivations for purchasing garden tractors. Therefore it does not affect T1.

final.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for small-scale landscaping, leveraging Deere’s tractor engineering. The evidence shows growing demand for garden tractors as inexpensive, practical tools for small gardens, and the company already produced a consumer model in 1963. A test should measure willingness to pay and purchase intent for a convenience‑focused model versus a status‑focused one.
final.target_customer: Individual homeowners with small gardens (approximately 30‑55 years old) who need a single tool for landscaping and yard work.
final.value_proposition: A durable, easy‑to‑use garden tractor built on Deere’s engineering, positioned as a convenient, one‑time purchase that saves time and labor compared to multiple tools.
final.next_action: Run the proposed Consumer Proposition Preference Test (500 homeowners, 8 weeks, €15,000) to compare willingness to pay and purchase intent for a convenience‑focused model versus a status‑focused one.
final.uncertainty: The size of the small‑scale landscaping market and whether homeowners will pay a premium for a consumer model are uncertain. The test will resolve these uncertainties.
would_change_if: If the test shows the status‑focused model achieving higher willingness to pay and purchase intent than the convenience‑focused model, we would reconsider the investment and explore a status‑positioned proposition.
If the test yields no significant difference between the two models, we would recommend no expansion and continue focusing on the existing B2B2C model.

arguments.name: Consumer Proposition Preference Test
arguments.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios and stated reasons.
arguments.sample: 500 U.S. homeowners aged 30-55, recruited via panels, balanced across regions with varying garden sizes.
arguments.measure: 1) Willingness to pay (WTP) for a consumer‑focused garden tractor. 2) Primary purchase reason (convenience vs. status). 3) Intent to purchase (binary: would buy).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher WTP and purchase intent among homeowners with small gardens and those citing convenience as primary reason.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher WTP and purchase intent among middle‑class homeowners and those citing status as primary reason.

arguments.decision_rule: If the average WTP for the convenience‑focused model exceeds the WTP for the status‑focused model by at least 15% and the purchase intent difference is at least 10 percentage points, proceed with the differentiated consumer proposition. Otherwise, do not invest.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

arguments.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for small-scale landscaping, leveraging Deere’s tractor engineering. The evidence shows growing demand for garden tractors as inexpensive, practical tools for small gardens, and the company already produced a consumer model in 1963. A test should measure willingness to pay and purchase intent for a convenience‑focused model versus a status‑focused one.

arguments.target_customer: Individual homeowners with small gardens (approximately 30‑55 years old) who need a single tool for landscaping and yard work.
arguments.value_proposition: A durable, easy‑to‑use garden tractor built on Deere’s engineering, positioned as a convenient, one‑time purchase that saves time and labor compared to multiple tools.
arguments.next_action: Run the proposed Consumer Proposition Preference Test (500 homeowners, 8 weeks, €15,000) to compare willingness to pay and purchase intent for a convenience‑focused model versus a status‑focused one.
arguments.uncertainty: The size of the small‑scale landscaping market and whether homeowners will pay a premium for a consumer model are uncertain. The test will resolve these uncertainties.
would_change_if: If the test shows the status‑focused model achieving higher willingness to pay and purchase intent than the convenience‑focused model, we would reconsider the investment and explore a status‑positioned proposition.
If the test yields no significant difference between the two models, we would recommend no expansion and continue focusing on the existing B2B2C model.
